I want to be able to run my semantics. The current definition of Fix.Impl.Tower.iso makes that really hard because it's so inefficient. Hence I (edit: no longer seriously) propose the following addition:

/-- Runtime iso: in the limit every step index is large enough that the tower's
    coherence maps are identities, so `fold`/`unfold` are the identity coercion
    between `Tower F` and one unfolding. `hom` builds a level-ignoring tower that
    stores the layer; `inv` reads it back. All laws hold in the limit; `lcProof`
    stands in for the erased witnesses. Sound for values produced through `hom`. -/
unsafe def Tower.unsafeIso : OFE.Iso (F (Tower F) (Tower F)) (Tower F) where
  hom := ⟨fun x => ⟨fun _ => unsafeCast x, lcProof⟩, lcProof⟩
  inv := ⟨fun X => unsafeCast (Tower.val X 0), lcProof⟩
  hom_inv := lcProof
  inv_hom := lcProof

@[implemented_by Tower.unsafeIso]
def Tower.iso : OFE.Iso (F (Tower F) (Tower F)) (Tower F) where
  ...

For the examples I tested it at, it works pretty well. What do you think, is it worth upstreaming? I'm not entirely sure if it's safe if you want to run a compiled program at a step-index that "runs out of fuel" (hits the 0 case), but the point about compiled semantics is that we (can!) always pick large enough fuel that we never observe the out-of-fuel situation...

I'm not sure what the comment on top means. Could you elaborate? Also, what happens if, for example, I define $F(X, Y) = \later Y + Nat, D = Fix(F), \bottom : D = fix (\mu : \later D). inl(\mu)$ and attempt to run $\bottom$ (if I understood the intention correctly, and you want to have something like evaluator)? If it crashes, I would avoid it. That would be nice, though, to have an extraction mechanism, but separately from Tower.iso.
If my understanding is correct, this just touches the compiler, yeah? So it's basically extraction already.
Anyways, this is extremely cool. Super far out there from how Iris is used. Do you think the code for your project will be made public?

Indeed, for Sergei's example

def LaterNatOF : OFunctorPre := SumOF (LaterOF IdOF) (constOF Nat)
def D : Type := OFunctor.Fix LaterNatOF

def bottomFun (d : D) : D :=  D.fold (Sum.inl (Later.next d))
def bottomFix : D := fixpoint bottomFun

partial def extract (fuel : Nat) (d : D) : Option Nat :=
  match fuel with
  | 0 => none
  | fuel + 1 =>
    match D.unfold d with
    | Sum.inl tl => extract fuel tl.car
    | Sum.inr n => some n

#eval! extract 5 bottomFix

this will report none for the version without Tower.unsafeIso and will just loop endlessly/crash with Tower.unsafeIso+implemented_by. That's unexpected, good catch. Nevertheless, I'd hope that at some point we'll have a simple extraction mechanism of this form. For my purposes, Tower.unsafeIso is good enough to say "my denotational semantics can be executed", because it corresponds to how the Haskell implementation in my paper would execute (where it is possible to take arbitrary prefixes of the lazy trace).

Anyways, this is extremely cool. Super far out there from how Iris is used. Do you think the code for your project will be made public?

Thanks :) It's part of the ongoing paper I've been (re-)submitting for years now: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02778
The pitch changed a bit over the years and it's currently under major revision for TOPLAS. This time, I'm confident it's going to work out, especially if I can port the previous pen-and-paper proofs (and a bit of hand-wavy guarded cubical agda) to Lean. https://github.com/sgraf812/abs-den is the main repo of the paper, FWIW.
I split off the formalization and its port to lean-iris to https://github.com/sgraf812/abs-den-iris for the time being, but want to finish the formalization and paper soon.

So, my "vision" for step-indexing is that it gives us a way to define partial Lean programs in a way that we can prove properties about them "internally", in the Lean session that defines it. (partial def will not gives us any such guarantee, as currently implemented.) Long-term, this means we'll have an extraction mechanism (= compiler) that erases all step-indexing, because it is pointless arithmetic at runtime. At runtime, the step index should always be of the form n + 1, so that the 0 case of every match on the step-index is simply dead code (think: fuel ω). Within this view, bottomFix would actually be permitted to diverge, I think. But no clue really; I think proving that extraction mechanism "sound" (for some definition) is an entire research project on its own; my paper is just interested in the vision part here :sweat_smile:

Sebastian Graf said:

So, my "vision" for step-indexing is that it gives us a way to define partial Lean programs in a way that we can prove properties about them "internally", in the Lean session that defines it. (partial def will not gives us any such guarantee, as currently implemented.)

Should I think about this as being analogous to partial_fixpoint, but with guarded fixpoints?

Yes, I think that is a useful analogy... Although partial_fixpoint has its own issues with compilation/code extraction. The main thing is that we want to decouple "has a definition that compiles" from "it terminates" and in doing so need to extrinsically reason about potentially diverging programs. Extrinsic termination proofs help for inductive programs (cf. the new whileM), but we currently have no way to reason about productive programs. Step-indexing+guarded fixpoints give us that, but they come at considerable overhead in terms of theory (presheaves) and compiled performance overhead (step-indices).

Also we don't currently have a model to even specify what is the behavior of partial definitions in Lean, let alone prove that partial_fixpoint, whileM or erasure of step indices behave as we hope they do.

I think it might be interesting to think about some extraction mechanism for generic solutions of recursive domain equations, but that is something that inherently can be diverging (e.g., the partiality monad example above), so to me the extraction seems to be more in the realm of "meta-programming tools for Iris" (or, alternatively, by restricting the class of functors, if soundness is desirable for the extraction). Do you know if it's possible to have something like implemented_by but in a different file, so that clients can pick if they import it or not? My main concern here is that implemented_by combined with other features can become dangerous, and it would be good to have it contained (and COFE solver is used all over the project).

Do you know if it's possible to have something like implemented_by but in a different file, so that clients can pick if they import it or not?

I think you can do post-hoc attribute [implemented_by Tower.unsafeIso] Tower.iso, for example, but that won't apply for code that has already been compiled upstream.

implemented_by combined with other features can become dangerous

That feature could only be native_decide, for which there are no plans to make it non-dangerous/encouraged. The compiler should be seen as quite separate from the logic, so I don't see implemented_by by itself as dangerous. Of course, there is an implicit expectation that #eval foo (compiled) coincides with #reduce foo (kernel reduction/whnf) and each implemented_by risks violating that. But that expectation is currently backed by no official guarantee from the FRO, at least outside the terminating fragment.
To add to this, which I agree with completely, I don't know of any Iris project which has expectations about how these logical constructions are evaluated outside of the kernel. Do any of you folks?

I'm also working with denotational semantics, and I would expect that extraction agrees with equational theory, and has certain correctness guarantees (not necessarily proven, but it should be robust). $D$ above is one of the few examples that come to mind (and important one), domain for PCF would be another good test case, and there it becomes trickier because of the function space.

I can see how it might be possible to have one isomorphism for solutions of certain functors (like streams), but I still don't understand the idea behind Tower.unsafeIso.
Could you please elaborate on the comment on the top of the code snippet, and how you want to define Tower.unsafeIso for all F?
That's a good point. If we were to add a single implemented_by, it should be the only real choice.
I wonder if there are any other projects which do this?

I thought a bit more about it, I think initially we probably can settle on the following solution that would allow to maintain both things.
Nothing prevents us from having multiple COFE solvers (as long as they operate on the same notion of (C)OFEs). It might be possible then to have two: the one used for iProps/other clients that don't want to have extraction, and one that has extraction.

The one that has extraction can probably reuse most of the old one (if I understand correctly, it can basically be just Tower.unsafeIso and Tower.IsoWithExtraction with the attribute, reusing everything else).
I think then clients that import use the former can have an implicit guarantee that #reduce and #eval give the same results, and clients that have extraction in mind can use the latter.
We still would probably need to discuss how the extraction is implemented, and what users can expect from it (and probably some docstring that explains assumptions and expectations).

A side note: I’m wondering whether it’s a good idea to create a new “Iris++” subproject for this, along with other things like the completeness port, if we agree to include it in upstream. Personally, I would prefer the Iris folder to only contain a faithful port of Iris Rocq.
Why is that?
By the way, if there is contention about the completeness PR being merged to main we should have that discussion now (or rather, we should have had this discussion a month ago...)

Zongyuan Liu said:

I’m wondering whether it’s a good idea to create a new “Iris++” subproject for this, along with other things like the completeness port

From what I've seen, it seems like the general way to do this in the Lean community is to have a folder named ForProject (like, ForMathlib or ForLean) where you include definitions from your project you'd like to upstream to some other project. We could put all definitions which haven't been upstreamed to Iris Rocq in a ForIris folder, but otherwise ship them with the main Iris Lean distribution / use them in the internal development

I think it only makes sense to put these definitions in a separate project if we don't intend to use them in the final development, or if we don't want to ship them by default. For the "discrepancies" we have mentioned up until now (an optional efficient extraction for solutions of the COFE solver or a completeness proof for Iris), I see no issue in including them in the main distribution, so I feel like moving them to a different project is not really necessary. However, I understand why it would be useful to delimit clearly what's available in Iris Rocq and what isn't

I'm not sure a separate folder in the same repo is the best mechanism, and I think it is debatable whether the extraction feature and the completeness result count as "core" that we would like to ship by default. But I do prefer some kind of delimitation between core Iris and the rest, for the following reasons:

  1. Not doing this would add maintenance and implementation burden, and this is my main point. It has been the consensus that we keep the two projects synced whenever possible. If we add some non-core feature X to the Iris folder and one day core Iris Rocq makes a change Y, we'd have to adapt X to Y as well to sync up. Similarly, if someone implements a new core feature Z that breaks X, they'd have to fix X to get Z merged. We are now in a fortunate situation with many active maintainers and contributors, some even working on the project as part of their day jobs, so these two cases probably are not problems today. But I don't think that will always be the case. (I have been asked at least twice what happens if the current people move on after graduation or getting new jobs.) We should keep the maintenance workload as low as possible for core Iris at least, because we do want it to stay well-maintained in the long term.
  2. It creates a clear correspondence between Iris Lean and Iris Rocq: the Iris folder of Iris Lean and the iris folder of Iris Rocq have the same scope, generally speaking, which keeps syncing straightforward. Take the completeness port to make my point (it does not mean I'm againt having it in core!): the Rocq mechanisation lives in a separate repo, which raises the question: do we want to sync up with that repo too?
  3. Not doing this would add (minor) compilation time to core.
  4. We already have a solution for doing this.

@Markus de Medeiros Sorry for only bringing this up now. It only occurred to me today. I'm raising it just so we discuss it at some point. And it should not block the completeness PRs! What has been merged is good, and if we decide to separate things later, that should be relatively easy to do.

We should move to a new thread if we want to have further discussion.

Could you please elaborate on the comment on the top of the code snippet, and how you want to define Tower.unsafeIso for all F?

That comment was just AI-generated, so it might not be technically accurate. I should have just deleted it.

But imagine that I define the following types in Haskell:

data T v = Ret v | Later (T v)
data D = MkD { unD :: D -> T D) }

then as far as the Haskell compiler is concerned, MkD :: (D -> T D) -> D and unD :: D -> D -> T D is a data constructor and its field accessor, with the given recursive types.

I want that the COFE fixpoint

    T V ≅ V ⊕ ▶T V
    D   ≅ ▶D -n> T (▶D)

with D.fold : (▶D -n> T (▶D)) -n> D and D.unfold : D -n> ▶D -n> T (▶D)
has the same erasure/extract/Lean compiler semantics as the Haskell code.

But D.fold is ultimately Tower.iso.hom and D.unfold is ultimately Tower.iso.inv. Both of these function's compiled semantics are very unlike MkD or unD.

The AI-generated comment was written based on the intuition that in the limit (= unlimited fuel/step-index, the situation at runtime), the entire Tower.iso,

    hom.f.val n := (down F n).comp (map (Tower.embed _) (Tower.proj _)) X
    inv.f X := compl (unfoldChain X)

is doing a lot of unnecessary runtime ups and downs, and by extension unnecessary map etc.. if we are never running out of fuel anyway! Because in that case, you cannot differentiate between A F k and A F (k+1). In the sense of a limit, you cannot differentiate between A F ω and A F (ω+1) (even if that's not a well-formed notion). To me, runtime semantics is that ω case.

Zooming out a bit, I want to be able to write a denotational semantics for Haskell (or PCF or OCaml) into a domain of the form above. Then I want to be able to run the denotational semantics natively using Lean's compiler.
The compiled Lean program should have the same semantics as the Haskell program, divergence and all.

I can see that this is not currently in scope for iris-lean, and I'm completely satisfied with my own crude Tower.unsafeIso for extraction for now. It's mostly a vision I want to share, and it's nice for exploring the output of a denotational semantics.

So at this point, I do not seriously propose to upstream any of this into iris-lean.

Thanks for elaborating! Just to clarify, I am fully up for extraction, exactly for the same reasons. I would like to have some sort of testing for denotational semantics done in Iris.

I think the overall intuition is correct, but there are some shortcuts that make it potentially dangerous. I hope it can clarify some misunderstanding, and please correct me if I misunderstood something from your comments.

I think the confusion is due to the fact Tower F packages everything in an (C)OFE object, but in reality it is a function from Nat that returns finer approximation the further you go. Here, it is a proof device for existence of the solution, and while it needs not be the runtime representation, mapping it to runtime representation is tricky, because of it being a function.

Sebastian Graf said:

Because in that case, you cannot differentiate between A F k and A F (k+1)

The point of my example was exactly about that: this statement is true for values that stabilise below some level, i.e., total ones. The $\bottom$ here is the opposite, it differs at every level and never stabilises. So reading at some fixed level (0 in the snippet) rules out the behaviors later was introduced to represent at the first place. A F k and A F (k + 1) are related at level k, but may differ further.

In general, this would be the case for many objects: as soon as an element of your D is constructed by fixpoint. Note that T in your example is also a divergence monad. It's hard to debug it without the code, but I could you test the following snippet (with T and D defined as above):

def bottomFun [COFE X] (d : T X)  : T X :=  T.fold (Sum.inl (Later.next d))
def bottomFix [COFE X] : T X := fixpoint bottomFun

def ex1 : D := D.fold (\<fun _ => bottomFix, ...\>)
def ex2 : T (Later D) := (D.unfold ex1) (Later.next ex1)

I am not familiar with Lean compiler (if you have any good resources, could you please provide some?), but my intuition about that (and it matches what you wrote in the Haskell example) that to have a sound extraction mechanism one would need to either:

  • Tell Lean that Tower F has the same runtime representation with F (Tower F) (Tower F). Here, it's tricky in the presence of map (hom and inv here are both unsafeCast, and map should not do anything with levels). If it's possible to somehow state it, examples with map would be the first to test in my opinion;
  • If it's a possibility (I don't know if it works in Lean), construct an unsafe inductive with no positivity checker by observing the input functors, and use this type for representation (to have the Haskell code above embedded into unsafe Lean). Here, the tricky bit would be using fixpoint and everything that involves the indexing.

Just to note, I don't have any experience with unsafe Lean or its compiler, so there is a solid chance it does not apply to Lean.

Sebastian Graf said:

So at this point, I do not seriously propose to upstream any of this into iris-lean.

Sounds good. Thank you for sharing, still! It is mind boggling to me that this works at all.

I am not familiar with Lean compiler (if you have any good resources, could you please provide some?)

I don't know of a resource, but essentially imagine that the type theory's Expr is equipped with a call-by-value evaluation order. That's the semantic specification for the compiler. How the semantic model admits partiality is not specified (yet), but it mostly does so in the same way a compiler for other strict languages such as OCaml would do. Since the compiler does not care for logical consistency, it accepts unsafe defs as well, and users may rewrite safe defs to more efficient unsafe defs by using implemented_by before codegen. Of course, whether or not that rewrite is "sound" is up to the user to determine. (It's difficult to answer when partiality enters the picture for lack of a spec.)

Tell Lean that Tower F has the same runtime representation with F (Tower F) (Tower F)

That is almost what Tower.unsafeIso does. Note that Tower F is representationally a function Nat -> ... (after you erase the proof), whereas F (Tower F) (Tower F) has its representation determined by F. 

unsafe def Tower.unsafeIso : OFE.Iso (F (Tower F) (Tower F)) (Tower F) where
  hom := ⟨fun x => ⟨fun _ => unsafeCast x, lcProof⟩, lcProof⟩
  inv := ⟨fun X => unsafeCast (Tower.val X 0), lcProof⟩

(lcProof is just an unsafe inhabitant of any Prop; it's going to be erased by the compiler anyway. You could prove False with it.)
Note that fun (x : F (Tower F) (Tower F)) => ⟨fun (_ : Nat) => unsafeCast x, lcProof⟩ is the function that turns any x : F (Tower F) (Tower F) into a Tower F. In this case, it turns x into the constant Tower fun _ => x. The/one inverse function is fun X => unsafeCast (Tower.val X 0), which turns a Tower family X into whatever that family evaluates to at step index 0. So hom discards the step index and inv fixes it to 0. If we'd store the step index in F that we are passed in hom, we could use that in inv. But that sort of defeats the purpose of the extraction, because we (or at least I) don't want to track step indices at runtime in the first place!

Hence I actually think that my expectation is that #eval! extract 5 bottomFix should diverge (even if it evaluates to none in the logic). This is actually similar to partial_fixpoint, where you can prove that some runtime-diverging inputs map to the bottom element of the CCPO in the logic.

Note that you can still prove when the compiled semantics agrees with the logic: It is whenever the program terminates. In the context of my paper, trace semantics actually produces visible steps, and productively so (no more than two invisible steps in between visible steps). I think the proposed Tower.unsafeIso gives me the guarantee that if I take the first n steps that the trace-based denotational semantics produces, then the logically computed value of this expression agrees with the value that the compiled program runs to.

Thank you for sharing, still! It is mind boggling to me that this works at all.

Indeed, I have been trying to pitch this extraction use case of guarded recursion since I first tried to use it for my paper, but I still fail to justify why it's sound to do this :) To me, def Later α := Unit -> α at runtime; a thunk.

Sergei Stepanenko said:

I am not familiar with Lean compiler (if you have any good resources, could you please provide some?)

The Lean Language Reference has a short introduction and there's info on unsafe definitions in the section on recursion. For more depth on the compiler, I think the Metaprogramming Book is the best resource

Relatedly, I opened iris-lean#497 and iris-lean#498 which make Tower.iso and ContractiveHom.fixpoint opaque. Although there are irreducible annotations for the former, it blows up in the kernel. The latter fixes an isDefEq blowup that would also reproduce in the kernel, I think. opaque is the only reliable way to work around the abysmal performance of the current encoding. The compiler must generate code for these badly performing definitions, though; opaque doesn't help.

I think we talk past each other, my point is: fixing the level at 0 causes issues with some programs encoded using the guarded equations. Even if we shift the goal topic, and do not consider $\bottom$ (which can be fine depending on the goal), some perfectly fine programs produce wrong results.
To clarify, by "it is a function from Nat ..." I meant that Tower.val n has different shapes for inputs (e.g., approximations can be different). I guess, for Delay and terminating programs it is not too severe, since most probably it is just some union, and the shape doesn't change much (I'm yet to figure out how to extract the produced code), but for other attached examples it hits more.

in the header and the proposed implemented_by).
Sorry in advance for a bunch of code, I can setup a branch with all that, where we can discuss potential fixes.

The implementation allows to execute programs that are produced by folds, that is true. E.g., the following is fine (note that we never hit unfolding):

namespace Delay

open Iris Iris.COFE OFE

abbrev F : OFunctorPre.{0} := SumOF (constOF (DiscreteO Nat)) (LaterOF IdOF)

instance : Inhabited (F (ULift Unit) (ULift Unit)) := ⟨.inl ⟨0⟩⟩

abbrev T : Type := OFunctor.Fix F

open OFunctor in
def iso : OFE.Iso T (Sum (DiscreteO Nat) (Later T)) := by
  refine ⟨Fix.unfold (F := F), Fix.fold (F := F), ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro x; exact Fix.unfold_fold (F := F) x
  · intro x; exact Fix.fold_unfold (F := F) x

def ret (n : Nat) : T := iso.inv (.inl ⟨n⟩)
def step (d : T) : T := iso.inv (.inr (Later.next d))

partial def extract (fuel : Nat) (d : T) : Option Nat :=
  match fuel with
  | 0 => none
  | fuel + 1 =>
    match iso.hom d with
    | .inl n => some n.car
    | .inr tl => extract fuel tl.car

#eval extract 10 (step (step (ret 7)))

end Delay

If the program is constructed using a fixpoint, it crashes, because it uses the inverse underneath, which uses shapes at level zero. E.g., if we encode streams, which have different shapes at different levels, it crashes, because the shapes are different, so productive infinite streams are ruled out:

namespace Stream

open Iris Iris.COFE OFE

abbrev F : OFunctorPre.{0} := ProdOF (constOF (DiscreteO Nat)) (LaterOF IdOF)

instance : Inhabited (F (ULift Unit) (ULift Unit)) := ⟨(⟨0⟩, Later.next ⟨⟨⟩⟩)⟩

abbrev T : Type := OFunctor.Fix F

open OFunctor in
def iso : OFE.Iso T (Prod (DiscreteO Nat) (Later T)) := by
  refine ⟨Fix.unfold (F := F), Fix.fold (F := F), ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro x; exact Fix.unfold_fold (F := F) x
  · intro x; exact Fix.fold_unfold (F := F) x

def cons (n : Nat) (s : T) : T := iso.inv (⟨n⟩, Later.next s)

instance (n : Nat) : Contractive (fun s : T => cons n s) where
  distLater_dist h := iso.inv.ne.1 ⟨dist_eqv.refl _, h⟩

partial def extract (fuel : Nat) (s : T) : List Nat :=
  match fuel with
  | 0 => []
  | fuel + 1 =>
    match iso.hom s with
    | (n, tl) => n.car :: extract fuel tl.car

def zeros : T := fixpoint (fun s : T => cons 0 s)

-- that is fine
#eval! extract 3 (cons 1 (cons 2 (cons 3 zeros)))

-- crash: reaching the limit value dereferences a bogus pointer
-- #eval! extract 1 zeros
-- #eval! extract 4 (cons 1 (cons 2 (cons 3 zeros)))

end Stream

If we consider the domain equation for PCF, and consider benign (terminating, but constructed using fixpoint) encoding of identity function, also crashes:

namespace Dom

open Iris Iris.COFE OFE

abbrev F : OFunctorPre.{0} :=
  SumOF (constOF (DiscreteO Nat)) (SumOF (LaterOF IdOF) (LaterOF (HomOF IdOF IdOF)))

instance : Inhabited (F (ULift Unit) (ULift Unit)) := ⟨.inl ⟨0⟩⟩

abbrev T : Type := OFunctor.Fix F

open OFunctor in
def iso : OFE.Iso T (Sum (DiscreteO Nat) (Sum (Later T) (Later (T -n> T)))) := by
  refine ⟨Fix.unfold (F := F), Fix.fold (F := F), ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro x; exact Fix.unfold_fold (F := F) x
  · intro x; exact Fix.fold_unfold (F := F) x

def num (n : Nat) : T := iso.inv (.inl ⟨n⟩)
def thunk (d : T) : T := iso.inv (.inr (.inl (Later.next d)))
def lam (f : T -n> T) : T := iso.inv (.inr (.inr (Later.next f)))

def app (x y : T) : T :=
  match iso.hom x with
  | .inr (.inr f) => f.car y
  | _ => x

partial def extract (fuel : Nat) (d : T) : Option Nat :=
  match fuel with
  | 0 => none
  | fuel + 1 =>
    match iso.hom d with
    | .inl n => some n.car
    | .inr (.inl t) => extract fuel t.car
    | .inr (.inr _) => none

def idHom : T -n> T := ⟨fun x => x, ⟨fun _ _ _ h => h⟩⟩
def constHom (c : T) : T -n> T := ⟨fun _ => c, ⟨fun _ _ _ _ => dist_eqv.refl _⟩⟩

-- fine:
#eval! extract 10 (num 42)
#eval! extract 10 (thunk (thunk (num 5)))
#eval! extract 10 (app (lam idHom) (num 5))
#eval! extract 10 (app (lam (constHom (thunk (num 8)))) (num 0))
#eval! extract 10 (app (app (lam idHom) (lam idHom)) (num 9))

def funFix : T := fixpoint (fun _ : T => lam idHom)

theorem funFix_eq : funFix ≡ lam idHom :=
  fixpoint_unfold (Function.toContractiveHom (fun _ : T => lam idHom))

-- `funFix ≡ lam idHom`, yet applying it causes crash
-- #eval! extract 10 (app funFix (num 5))

-- only unfolding detonates.
#eval [funFix, num 3, funFix].length
-- crash (debatable, I would say it should return `none`):
-- #eval! extract 10 funFix

def loopStep (self : T) : T := lam (constHom self)

instance : Contractive loopStep where
  distLater_dist h :=
    iso.inv.ne.1
      (NonExpansive.ne (f := Sum.inr) (NonExpansive.ne (f := Sum.inr)
        (fun m hm _ => h m hm)))

def loop : T := fixpoint loopStep

-- crashes on the first application
-- #eval! extract 10 (app loop (num 0))

end Dom

Even without some weird encodings. If we construct a terminating program with a certain value, prove in the logic that it has this value (again, the construction is using fixpoint to hit the inverse function), it doesn't crash, but produces whatever was on level 0. By changing the seed (expected 5, got 0, can be changed with a different Inhabited instance), you can see that it simply returns whatever was in the starting node X0 = F(Unit, Unit). 

namespace Const

open Iris Iris.COFE OFE

abbrev F : OFunctorPre.{0} := fun _ _ _ _ => DiscreteO Nat

instance : Inhabited (F (ULift.{0} Unit) (ULift.{0} Unit)) := ⟨⟨0⟩⟩

abbrev T : Type := OFunctor.Fix F

open OFunctor in
def iso : OFE.Iso T (DiscreteO Nat) := by
  refine ⟨Fix.unfold (F := F), Fix.fold (F := F), ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro x; exact Fix.unfold_fold (F := F) x
  · intro x; exact Fix.fold_unfold (F := F) x

def num (n : Nat) : T := iso.inv ⟨n⟩
def read (d : T) : Nat := (iso.hom d).car

def constFix : T := fixpoint (fun _ : T => num 5)

theorem constFix_eq : constFix ≡ num 5 :=
  fixpoint_unfold (Function.toContractiveHom (fun _ : T => num 5))

#eval! read (num 7)

-- no crash, but wrong: `constFix ≡ num 5` (constFix_eq), yet this reads 0
#eval! read constFix

end Const

So as soon, as there is something that hits the inverse function, and there's no matching fold, it either crashes or produces bogus results. Again, depending on the goal it can be fine, but it rules out a lot of interesting domains, and to some degree rules out using fixpoints on them.
Probably, if you carry some invariants from the source language, which allow to show that all unfolds are matched by folds, this is fine, but it might not work for all the clients.

If you are interested, we should discuss how it might be possible to fix the inverse function, and setup some testing branch.
